{{Short description|Finance model linking expected return to systematic risk}}
[[File:Security market line of CAPM.svg|thumb|right|350px|'''Security market line (SML)''': The SML displays the expected rate of return of an individual security as a function of systematic, non-diversifiable risk (Beta).]]

In finance, the [[capital asset pricing model]] ('''CAPM''') is a model used to determine a theoretically appropriate required rate of return of an asset, to make decisions about adding assets to a well-diversified portfolio.<ref name="Sharpe1964">{{cite journal |last=Sharpe |first=William F. |year=1964 |title=Capital Asset Prices: A Theory of Market Equilibrium under Conditions of Risk |journal=Journal of Finance |volume=19 |issue=3 |pages=425–442 |doi=10.1111/j.1540-6261.1964.tb02865.x}}</ref> The model takes into account the asset's sensitivity to non-diversifiable risk (also known as [[systematic risk]] or market risk), often represented by the quantity [[beta (finance)|beta]] (β) in the financial industry, as well as the expected return of the market and the expected return of a theoretical risk-free asset.<ref name="Lintner1965">{{cite journal |last=Lintner |first=John |year=1965 |title=The Valuation of Risk Assets and the Selection of Risky Investments in Stock Portfolios and Capital Budgets |journal=Review of Economics and Statistics |volume=47 |issue=1 |pages=13–37 |doi=10.2307/1924119}}</ref>

CAPM assumes a particular form of utility functions (in which only first and second moments matter, that is risk is measured by variance, for example a quadratic utility) or alternatively asset returns whose probability distributions are completely described by the first two moments (for example, the normal distribution) and zero transaction costs (necessary for diversification to get rid of all idiosyncratic risk).<ref name="Mossin1966">{{cite journal |last=Mossin |first=Jan |year=1966 |title=Equilibrium in a Capital Asset Market |journal=Econometrica |volume=34 |issue=4 |pages=768–783 |doi=10.2307/1910098}}</ref><ref name="Markowitz1952">{{cite journal |last=Markowitz |first=Harry |year=1952 |title=Portfolio Selection |journal=The Journal of Finance |volume=7 |issue=1 |pages=77–91 |doi=10.1111/j.1540-6261.1952.tb01525.x}}</ref> Under these conditions, CAPM shows that the cost of equity capital is determined only by beta.<ref name="Sharpe1964" /><ref name="Lintner1965" /> Despite its failing numerous empirical tests,<ref name="FamaFrench2004">{{cite journal |last1=Fama |first1=Eugene F. |last2=French |first2=Kenneth R. |date=2004 |title=The Capital Asset Pricing Model: Theory and Evidence |journal=Journal of Economic Perspectives |volume=18 |issue=3 |pages=25–46 |doi=10.1257/0895330042162430}}</ref> and the existence of more modern approaches to asset pricing and portfolio selection (such as [[arbitrage pricing theory]] and [[Merton's portfolio problem]]), the CAPM still remains popular due to its simplicity and utility in a variety of situations.<ref name="FamaFrench2004" />

== Inventors ==
The CAPM was introduced by economists [[Jack L. Treynor|Jack Treynor]] (1961, 1962),<ref name="Treynor1961">{{cite report |last=Treynor |first=Jack L. |year=1961 |title=Market Value, Time, and Risk |type=Unpublished manuscript}}</ref> [[William F. Sharpe]] (1964),<ref name="Sharpe1964" /> [[John Lintner]] (1965)<ref name="Lintner1965" /> and [[Jan Mossin]] (1966)<ref name="Mossin1966" /> independently, building on the earlier work of [[Harry Markowitz]] on diversification and [[modern portfolio theory]].<ref name="Markowitz1952" /> Sharpe, Markowitz and [[Merton Miller]] jointly received the 1990 [[Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences]] for this contribution to the field of financial economics.<ref name="Nobel1990">{{cite web |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/1990/summary/ |title=The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 1990 |publisher=Nobel Prize Outreach AB |access-date=2025-12-25}}</ref> [[Fischer Black]] (1972) developed another version of CAPM, called Black CAPM or zero-beta CAPM, that does not assume the existence of a riskless asset.<ref name="Black1972">{{cite journal |last=Black |first=Fischer |year=1972 |title=Capital Market Equilibrium with Restricted Borrowing |journal=Journal of Business |volume=45 |issue=3 |pages=444–454 |doi=10.1086/295472}}</ref> This version was more robust against empirical testing and was influential in the widespread adoption of the CAPM.<ref name="Black1972" />

== Black CAPM ==
'<nowiki/>''[[Fischer Black]] (1972) developed another version of CAPM, called Black CAPM''' or zero-beta CAPM, that does not assume the existence of a riskless asset.<ref name="Black1972">{{cite journal |last=Black |first=Fischer |year=1972 |title=Capital Market Equilibrium with Restricted Borrowing |journal=Journal of Business |volume=45 |issue=3 |pages=444–454 |doi=10.1086/295472}}</ref> This version replaces the risk-free rate with the return of a "zero-beta portfolio"—a portfolio that has no correlation with the market. This version was found to be more robust against empirical testing, particularly in explaining why the security market line is often flatter than the standard model predicts.<ref name="Black1972" />

== Formula ==
[[File:CAPM_Querschnitt_Zeitreihe2.png|left|thumb|400x400px|The Security Market Line (SML) showing the relationship between expected return E(Ri) and systematic risk (beta). Assets above the line carry a positive alpha.]]
The CAPM is a model for pricing an individual security or portfolio.<ref name="Sharpe196423">{{cite journal |last=Sharpe |first=William F. |year=1964 |title=Capital Asset Prices: A Theory of Market Equilibrium under Conditions of Risk |journal=Journal of Finance |volume=19 |issue=3 |pages=425–442}}</ref> For individual securities, it makes use of the security market line (SML) and its relation to expected return and systematic risk (beta) to show how the market must price individual securities in relation to their security risk class.<ref name="Lintner196544">{{cite journal |last=Lintner |first=John |year=1965 |title=The Valuation of Risk Assets and the Selection of Risky Investments in Stock Portfolios and Capital Budgets |journal=Review of Economics and Statistics |volume=47 |issue=1 |pages=13–37}}</ref>

The SML enables us to calculate the reward-to-risk ratio for any security in relation to that of the overall market.<ref name="Mossin1966233">{{cite journal |last=Mossin |first=Jan |year=1966 |title=Equilibrium in a Capital Asset Market |journal=Econometrica |volume=34 |issue=4 |pages=768–783}}</ref> Therefore, when the expected rate of return for any security is deflated by its beta coefficient, the reward-to-risk ratio for any individual security in the market is equal to the market reward-to-risk ratio, thus:<ref name="Sharpe196423" />

In equilibrium, all assets should plot directly on the SML. An asset located above the line is considered undervalued, as it offers a higher return for its level of systematic risk, while an asset below is overvalued. The slope of the SML represents the market risk premium, illustrating the trade-off between risk and return. By determining the position of a security relative to this line, investors can identify whether the expected return justifies the asset's market-related volatility.<ref name="FamaFrench2004533">{{cite journal |last1=Fama |first1=Eugene F. |last2=French |first2=Kenneth R. |year=2004 |title=The Capital Asset Pricing Model: Theory and Evidence |journal=Journal of Economic Perspectives |volume=18 |issue=3 |pages=25–46}}</ref>
{| class="wikitable" style="width:100%; line-height:1.5em;"
|+'''CAPM Mathematical Framework'''
! scope="col" style="background:#f2f2f2; width:20%;" |Component
! scope="col" style="background:#f2f2f2; width:35%;" |Equation / Derivation
! scope="col" style="background:#f2f2f2; width:45%;" |Description & Logic
|-
|'''Reward-to-Risk Ratio'''
|:<math>\frac{E(R_i) - R_f}{\beta_i} = E(R_m) - R_f</math>
|Shows that the risk premium per unit of beta is constant for all assets in the market.<ref name="Sharpe196423" /><ref name="Mossin1966233" />
|-
|'''Standard CAPM'''
|:<math>E(R_i) = R_f + \beta_i (E(R_m) - R_f)</math>
|Obtained by rearranging the reward-to-risk equation to solve for <math>E(R_i)</math>. This is the primary model for determining the required return of an asset<ref name="Lintner196544" />
|-
|'''Jensen's Alpha'''
|:<math>E(R_i) = R_f + \beta_i (E(R_m) - R_f) + \alpha_i</math>
|Measures the abnormal return of an asset. A positive <math>\alpha</math> indicates outperformance relative to the SML.<ref name="Jensen1968">{{cite journal |last=Jensen |first=Michael C. |year=1968 |title=The Performance of Mutual Funds in the Period 1945–1964 |journal=Journal of Finance |volume=23 |issue=2 |pages=389–416}}</ref>
|-
|'''Black CAPM'''
|:<math>E(R_i) = E(R_z) + \beta_i (E(R_m) - E(R_z))</math>
|A version for restricted borrowing; replaces <math>R_f</math> with the return of a zero-beta portfolio (<math>E(R_z)</math>).<ref name="Black19723">{{cite journal |last=Black |first=Fischer |year=1972 |title=Capital Market Equilibrium with Restricted Borrowing |journal=Journal of Business |volume=45 |pages=444–454}}</ref>
|-
|'''Beta Definition'''
|:<math>\beta_i = \frac{\text{Cov}(R_i, R_m)}{\text{Var}(R_m)} = \rho_{i,m} \frac{\sigma_i}{\sigma_m}</math>
|Measures the sensitivity of the expected excess asset returns to the expected excess market returns.<ref name="Sharpe196423" />
|
|-
| '''Risk Premium Form'''
| :<math>E(R_i) - R_f = \beta_i (E(R_m) - R_f)</math>
| Restates that the individual risk premium equals the market premium multiplied by beta; this form is often used in empirical testing to isolate the excess return.<ref name="Lintner196544" />
|}

== Modified betas ==
There has also been research into a mean-reverting beta often referred to as the adjusted beta,<ref name="Blume19712">{{cite journal |last=Blume |first=Marshall E. |year=1971 |title=On the Assessment of Risk |journal=The Journal of Finance |volume=26 |issue=1 |pages=1–10}}</ref> as well as the consumption beta.<ref name="Breeden19792">{{cite journal |last=Breeden |first=Douglas T. |year=1979 |title=An intertemporal asset pricing model |journal=Journal of Financial Economics |volume=7 |issue=3 |pages=265–296}}</ref> However, in empirical tests, the traditional CAPM has been found to do as well as or outperform these modified beta models.<ref name="FamaFrench20044">{{cite journal |last1=Fama |first1=Eugene F. |last2=French |first2=Kenneth R. |year=2004 |title=The CAPM: Theory and Evidence |journal=Journal of Economic Perspectives |volume=18 |pages=25–46}}</ref><ref name="MankiwShapiro19862">{{cite journal |last1=Mankiw |first1=N. Gregory |last2=Shapiro |first2=Matthew D. |year=1986 |title=Risk and return: Consumption beta versus market beta |journal=Review of Economics and Statistics |volume=68 |issue=3 |pages=452–459}}</ref> Specifically, research by Mankiw and Shapiro (1986) found that the market beta of the traditional CAPM outperformed the consumption beta in explaining the cross-section of stock returns.<ref name="MankiwShapiro19862" /> Furthermore, while the adjusted beta (Blume's method) improves forecast accuracy, it does not consistently resolve the underlying empirical failures of the model's predictive power over long horizons.<ref name="FamaFrench19923">{{cite journal |last1=Fama |first1=Eugene F. |last2=French |first2=Kenneth R. |year=1992 |title=The Cross-Section of Expected Stock Returns |journal=Journal of Finance |volume=47 |issue=2 |pages=427–465}}</ref>

== Security market line ==
The SML graphs the results from the capital asset pricing model (CAPM) formula.<ref name="Sharpe19643">{{cite journal |last=Sharpe |first=William F. |year=1964 |title=Capital Asset Prices |journal=Journal of Finance |volume=19 |issue=3 |pages=425–442}}</ref> The x-axis represents the risk (beta), and the y-axis represents the expected return.<ref name="Lintner19653">{{cite journal |last=Lintner |first=John |year=1965 |title=The Valuation of Risk Assets |journal=Review of Economics and Statistics |volume=47 |issue=1 |pages=13–37}}</ref> The market risk premium is determined from the slope of the SML.<ref name="Sharpe19643" />

The relationship between <math>\beta</math> and required return is plotted on the security market line (SML), which shows expected return as a function of <math>\beta</math>.<ref name="Mossin19663">{{cite journal |last=Mossin |first=Jan |year=1966 |title=Equilibrium in a Capital Asset Market |journal=Econometrica |volume=34 |issue=4 |pages=768–783}}</ref> The intercept is the nominal risk-free rate available for the market, while the slope is the market premium, <math>E(R_m) - R_f</math>.<ref name="Sharpe19643" /> The security market line can be regarded as representing a single-factor model of the asset price, where <math>\beta</math> is the exposure to changes in the value of the Market.<ref name="FamaFrench20043">{{cite journal |last1=Fama |first1=Eugene F. |last2=French |first2=Kenneth R. |year=2004 |title=The CAPM: Theory and Evidence |journal=Journal of Economic Perspectives |volume=18 |pages=25–46}}</ref>

: <math>\text{SML}: E(R_i) = R_f + \beta_i (E(R_M) - R_f)</math><ref name="Sharpe19643" />

It is a useful tool for determining if an asset being considered for a portfolio offers a reasonable expected return for its risk.<ref name="Lintner19653" /> Individual securities are plotted on the SML graph.<ref name="Sharpe19643" /> If the security's expected return versus risk is plotted above the SML, it is undervalued since the investor can expect a greater return for the inherent risk.<ref name="Sharpe19643" /> Conversely, a security plotted below the SML is overvalued since the investor would be accepting less return for the amount of risk assumed.<ref name="Sharpe19643" />

==Asset pricing==
Once the expected/required rate of return <math>E(R_i)</math> is calculated using CAPM, we can compare this required rate of return to the asset's estimated rate of return over a specific investment horizon to determine whether it would be an appropriate investment. To make this comparison, you need an independent estimate of the return outlook for the security based on either '''fundamental or technical analysis techniques''', including P/E, M/B etc.

Assuming that the CAPM is correct, an asset is correctly priced when its estimated price is the same as the present value of future cash flows of the asset, discounted at the rate suggested by CAPM. If the estimated price is higher than the CAPM valuation, then the asset is overvalued (and undervalued when the estimated price is below the CAPM valuation).<ref name="luenberger">{{cite book|title=Investment Science|last=Luenberger|first=David|publisher=Oxford University Press|year=1997}}</ref> When the asset does not lie on the SML, this could also suggest mis-pricing. Since the expected return of the asset at time <math>t</math> is <math>E(R_t)=\frac{E(P_{t+1})-P_t}{P_t}</math>, a higher expected return than what CAPM suggests indicates that <math>P_t</math> is too low (the asset is currently undervalued), assuming that at time <math>t+1</math> the asset returns to the CAPM suggested price.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bodie |first1=Z. |last2=Kane |first2=A. |last3=Marcus |first3=A. J. |title=Investments |edition=7th International |page=303 |location=Boston |publisher=McGraw-Hill |year=2008 }}</ref>

The asset price <math>P_0</math> using CAPM, sometimes called the certainty equivalent pricing formula, is a linear relationship given by
:<math>P_0 = \frac{1}{1 + R_f} \left[E(P_T) - \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(P_T,R_M)(E(R_M) - R_f)}{\mathrm{Var}(R_M)}\right]</math>
where <math>P_T</math> is the future price of the asset or portfolio.<ref name="luenberger" />

== Asset-specific required return ==
The CAPM returns the asset-appropriate required return or discount rate—the rate at which future cash flows produced by the asset should be discounted given that asset's relative riskiness.<ref name="Sharpe19645">{{cite journal |last=Sharpe |first=William F. |year=1964 |title=Capital Asset Prices |journal=Journal of Finance |volume=19 |issue=3 |pages=425–442}}</ref> Betas exceeding one signify more than average "riskiness", while betas below one indicate lower than average risk.<ref name="Lintner19655">{{cite journal |last=Lintner |first=John |year=1965 |title=The Valuation of Risk Assets |journal=Review of Economics and Statistics |volume=47 |issue=1 |pages=13–37}}</ref> Thus, a more risky stock will have a higher beta and will be discounted at a higher rate; less sensitive stocks will have lower betas and be discounted at a lower rate.<ref name="Sharpe19645" /> Given the accepted concave utility function, the CAPM is consistent with intuition that investors require a higher return for holding a more risky asset.<ref name="Mossin19665">{{cite journal |last=Mossin |first=Jan |year=1966 |title=Equilibrium in a Capital Asset Market |journal=Econometrica |volume=34 |issue=4 |pages=768–783}}</ref>

Since beta reflects asset-specific sensitivity to non-diversifiable market risk, the market as a whole, by definition, has a beta of one.<ref name="Sharpe19645" /> Stock market indices are frequently used as local proxies for the market—and in that case, by definition, have a beta of one.<ref name="FamaFrench20044" /> An investor in a large, diversified portfolio, such as a mutual fund designed to track the total market, therefore expects performance in line with the market.<ref name="Lintner19655" />

=== Fundamental Valuation (Present Value) ===
[[File:WACC-Ansatz.jpg|left|thumb|321x321px|The WACC approach: The cost of equity (derived from CAPM) and the cost of debt are weighted by their market proportions to determine the overall discount rate (<math>E(R_i)</math>).<ref name="IESE2010">Fernández, P. (2010). "WACC: Definition, Misconceptions and Errors," ''IESE Working Paper''.</ref>]]


Once the required expected return <math>E(R_i)</math> is established via CAPM, it is used as the discount rate to determine an asset's intrinsic value based on future [[cash flows]] (CF).<ref name="Damodaran2012">Damodaran, A. (2012). ''Investment Valuation'', Wiley.</ref>

The intrinsic value is calculated using the following present value formula:

: <math>PV = \sum_{t=1}^{n} \frac{E(CF_t)}{(1 + E(R_i))^t}</math>

An asset is considered '''undervalued''' if its calculated <math>Present Value</math> is higher than the current market price, and '''overvalued''' if the price exceeds this intrinsic value.<ref name="Graham1934">Graham, B. and Dodd, D. (1934). ''Security Analysis''.</ref>

|-

|The expected cash flow in period ''t''.<ref name="Damodaran2012" />
|-

==Risk and diversification==
The risk of a portfolio comprises [[systematic risk]], also known as undiversifiable risk, and [[unsystematic risk]], which is also known as idiosyncratic risk or diversifiable risk.<ref name="Markowitz19522">{{cite journal |last=Markowitz |first=Harry |year=1952 |title=Portfolio Selection |journal=The Journal of Finance |volume=7 |issue=1 |pages=77–91}}</ref> Systematic risk refers to the risk common to all securities—i.e., market risk.<ref name="Sharpe19645" /> Unsystematic risk is the risk associated with individual assets.<ref name="Markowitz19522" />

Unsystematic risk can be diversified away to smaller levels by including a greater number of assets in the portfolio as specific risks "average out".<ref name="Statman19872">{{cite journal |last=Statman |first=Meir |year=1987 |title=How Many Stocks Make a Diversified Portfolio? |journal=Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis |volume=22 |issue=3 |pages=353–363}}</ref> The same is not possible for systematic risk within one market.<ref name="Sharpe19645" /> Depending on the market, a portfolio of approximately 30–40 securities in developed markets such as the UK or US will render the portfolio sufficiently diversified such that risk exposure is limited to systematic risk only.<ref name="Statman19872" /> This number may vary depending on the way securities are weighted in a portfolio which alters the overall risk contribution of each security.<ref name="Markowitz19522" /> For example, market cap weighting means that securities of companies with larger market capitalization will take up a larger portion of the portfolio, making it effectively less diversified.<ref name="FamaFrench20044" /> In developing markets, a larger number of securities is required for diversification due to higher asset volatilities.<ref name="Statman19872" />

A rational investor should not take on any diversifiable risk, as only non-diversifiable risks are rewarded within the scope of this model.<ref name="Sharpe19645" /> Therefore, the required return on an asset must be linked to its contribution to overall portfolio riskiness as opposed to its "stand alone risk".<ref name="Lintner19655" /> In the CAPM context, portfolio risk is represented by higher variance—i.e., less predictability.<ref name="Markowitz19522" /> In other words, the beta of the portfolio is the defining factor in rewarding the systematic exposure taken by an investor.<ref name="Sharpe19645" />

==Efficient frontier==
The CAPM assumes that the risk-return profile of a portfolio can be optimized—an optimal portfolio displays the lowest possible level of risk for its level of return.<ref name="Markowitz19522" />

Additionally, since each additional asset introduced into a portfolio further diversifies the portfolio, the optimal portfolio must comprise every asset with each asset value-weighted to achieve efficiency.<ref name="Sharpe19645" /> This assumes no trading costs and that any asset is infinitely divisible.<ref name="Lintner19655" /> All such optimal portfolios, i.e., one for each level of return, comprise the efficient frontier.<ref name="Markowitz19522" /> Because the unsystematic risk is diversifiable, the total risk of a portfolio can be viewed as beta.<ref name="Sharpe19645" />

== Assumptions ==

All investors:<ref>{{cite book|last=Arnold|first=Glen|title=Corporate financial management|year=2005|publisher=Financial Times/Prentice Hall|page=354|edition=3.}}</ref>

# Aim to maximize economic utilities (Asset quantities are given and fixed).
# Are rational and risk-averse.
# Are broadly diversified across a range of investments.
# Are price takers, i.e., they cannot influence prices.
# Can lend and borrow unlimited amounts under the risk free rate of interest.
# Trade without transaction or taxation costs.
# Deal with securities that are all highly divisible into small parcels (All assets are perfectly divisible and liquid).
# Have homogeneous expectations.
# Have all information available all at the same time.

== Criticisms and Empirical Evidence ==
In their 2004 review, economists [[Eugene Fama]] and [[Kenneth French]] argue that "the failure of the CAPM in empirical tests implies that most applications of the model are invalid".<ref name="FamaFrench20042">{{cite journal |last1=Fama |first1=Eugene F. |last2=French |first2=Kenneth R. |date=2004 |title=The Capital Asset Pricing Model: Theory and Evidence |url=https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/0895330042162430 |journal=Journal of Economic Perspectives |volume=18 |issue=3 |pages=25–46 |doi=10.1257/0895330042162430 |access-date=2025-12-25}}</ref>

Despite its theoretical importance, the CAPM is often criticized for failing to match real-world market dynamics. The following table provides a comprehensive consolidation of empirical failures, theoretical inconsistencies, and behavioral critiques.

{| class="wikitable" style="width: 100%; font-size: 88%; line-height: 1.5em;"
|+ '''Consolidated Analysis of CAPM Critiques'''
! scope="col" style="width: 15%; background:#f2f2f2;" | Category
! scope="col" style="width: 25%; background:#f2f2f2;" | Specific Problem
! scope="col" style="width: 60%; background:#f2f2f2;" | Detailed Description, Mathematical Context, and References
|-
| rowspan="4" | '''Empirical & Statistical'''
| '''Low-Volatility Anomaly'''
| Data indicates the relationship between risk and return is flatter than predicted. Low-beta stocks offer higher returns than the model predicts, suggesting either the [[efficient-market hypothesis]] is wrong or the CAPM is incorrect.<ref name="FamaFrench1992">{{cite journal|last1=Fama|first1=E.|last2=French|first2=K.|title=The Cross-Section of Expected Stock Returns|journal=Journal of Finance|volume=47|issue=2|pages=427–465|year=1992}}</ref><ref name="Baltussen2024">{{cite journal|last1=Baltussen|first1=G.|last2=van Vliet|first2=B.|last3=van Vliet|first3=P.|title=The Cross-Section of Stock Returns before CRSP|journal=SSRN Working Paper|year=2024}}</ref><ref name="Blitz2019">{{cite journal|last1=Blitz|first1=D.|last2=Van Vliet|first2=P.|title=The volatility effect revisited|journal=Journal of Portfolio Management|volume=46|issue=1|year=2019}}</ref>
|-
| '''Predictive Accuracy'''
| The model relies on historical measurements which often fail to reflect future risk or new circumstances. Modern approaches attempt to use "future-risk" betas to resolve this.<ref name="French2016">{{cite journal|last=French|first=Jordan|title=Back to the Future Betas|journal=International Journal of Financial Studies|volume=4|issue=3|year=2016}}</ref><ref name="Markowitz2000">{{cite book|last=Markowitz|first=Harry|title=Mean-Variance Analysis in Portfolio Choice and Capital Markets|publisher=Wiley|year=2000}}</ref>
|-
| '''Non-Constant Risk'''
| While CAPM treats <math>\beta</math> as a static constant, empirical studies show that Beta is time-varying and sensitive to different market cycles.<ref name="FrenchTimeVarying">{{cite book|last1=French|first1=Jordan|title=Estimating Time-Varying Beta Coefficients|series=Research in Finance|volume=32|year=2016}}</ref>
|-
| '''Size & Value Effects'''
| Anomalies such as the historical outperformance of small-cap and value stocks are not captured by a single-factor beta, leading to multi-factor models.<ref name="FamaFrench1993">{{cite journal|last1=Fama|first1=E.F.|last2=French|first2=K.R.|title=Common Risk Factors in the Returns on Stocks and Bonds|journal=Journal of Financial Economics|volume=33|issue=1|pages=3–56|year=1993}}</ref>
|-
| rowspan="5" | '''Theoretical & Logical'''
| '''[[Richard Roll|Roll's]] Critique'''
| The "market portfolio" is unobservable as it should theoretically include all assets (real estate, human capital). Using stock indices as proxies can lead to false mathematical inferences.<ref name="Roll1977">{{cite journal|last=Roll|first=R.|title=A Critique of the Asset Pricing Theory's Tests|journal=Journal of Financial Economics|volume=4|issue=2|pages=129–176|year=1977}}</ref><ref name="Ibbotson1985">{{cite journal|last1=Ibbotson|first1=R.|last2=Siegel|first2=L.|title=World wealth: Market values and returns|journal=Journal of Portfolio Management|volume=12|year=1985}}</ref>
|-
| '''Circularity & Irrationality'''
| Critics argue the model is circular because the price of total risk is a function of covariance risk. Furthermore, identical discount rates are often found for different risk levels.<ref name="Dayala2012">{{cite journal|last=Dayala|first=Roger|year=2012|title=The Capital Asset Pricing Model: A Fundamental Critique|journal=Business Valuation Review|volume=31|issue=1}}</ref><ref name="LaiStohs2015">{{cite journal|last1=Lai|first1=T.Y.|last2=Stohs|first2=M.H.|year=2015|title=Yes, CAPM is dead|journal=International Journal of Business|volume=20}}</ref>
|-
| '''Measurement of Risk'''
| Assumes variance is the sole measure of risk, ignoring asymmetric downside risk. Investors may prioritize a "Safety-First" approach:
:<math>\text{Minimize } P(R < L)</math>
utilizing lower partial moments.<ref name="Roy1952">{{cite journal|last=Roy|first=A.D.|title=Safety-first and the holding of assets|journal=Econometrica|volume=20|year=1952}}</ref><ref name="Jansen2000">{{cite journal|last1=Jansen|first1=D.W.|last2=de Vries|first2=C.G.|title=Portfolio selection with limited downside risk|journal=Journal of Empirical Finance|volume=7|year=2000}}</ref>
|-
| '''Market Frictions'''
| The model assumes a frictionless world with no taxes, no transaction costs, and infinitely divisible assets, which does not match actual trading environments.<ref name="Elton2009">{{cite book|last1=Elton|first1=E.J.|last2=Gruber|first2=M.J.|title=Modern Portfolio Theory and Investment Analysis|year=2009}}</ref>
|-
| '''Horizon Misalignment'''
| The model assumes short-term optimization. Long-term investors may view inflation-linked bonds, rather than cash, as the true risk-free asset.<ref name="Campbell2002">{{cite book|last1=Campbell|first1=J.Y.|last2=Viceira|first2=L.M.|title=Strategic Asset Allocation|publisher=Oxford University Press|year=2002}}</ref>
|-
| rowspan="3" | '''Behavioral & Structural'''
| '''[[Behavioral Finance]]'''
| Psychological biases like overconfidence cause market inefficiencies that the linear CAPM cannot capture or explain.<ref name="Daniel2001">{{cite journal|last1=Daniel|first1=K.|last2=Hirshleifer|first2=D.|title=Overconfidence, Arbitrage, and Equilibrium Asset Pricing|journal=Journal of Finance|volume=56|year=2001}}</ref>
|-
| '''Mental Accounting'''
| Investors often hold fragmented portfolios for specific goals (e.g., retirement vs. speculation) rather than one single optimized portfolio.<ref name="Shefrin2000">{{cite journal|last1=Shefrin|first1=H.|last2=Statman|first2=M.|year=2000|title=Behavioral Portfolio Theory|journal=JFQA|volume=35}}</ref>
|-
| '''Skewness Preference'''
| Investors may accept lower returns for assets with high positive skewness (lottery effect). This is modeled by the Co-skewness CAPM:<ref name="Kraus1976">{{cite journal|last1=Kraus|first1=A.|last2=Litzenberger|first2=R.H.|year=1976|title=Skewness Preference and the Valuation of Risk Assets|journal=Journal of Finance|volume=31}}</ref>
:<math>E(R_i) - R_f = b_1 \beta + b_2 \frac{E[(R_i - \bar{R}_i)(R_m - \bar{R}_m)^2]}{E[(R_m - \bar{R}_m)^3]}</math>
|}
== Extensions of the CAPM ==
To address the empirical and theoretical limitations of the standard CAPM, several extensions have been developed that relax the model's core assumptions.

{| class="wikitable" style="width: 100%; max-width: 850px; font-size: 95%;"
|+ '''Key Extensions and Alternative Models'''
! Model !! Primary Adjustment !! Description and References
|-
| '''[[Intertemporal CAPM]] (ICAPM)'''
| Multi-period horizon
| Generalizes the model by allowing for multiple dates and repeated portfolio rebalancing.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Merton|first=R.C.|year=1973|title=An Intertemporal Capital Asset Pricing Model|journal=Econometrica|volume=41|issue=5|pages=867–887}}</ref>
|-
| '''[[Consumption-based capital asset pricing model|Consumption CAPM]] (CCAPM)'''
| Consumption utility
| Focuses on how an asset covaries with aggregate consumption rather than market wealth.<ref name=Breeden>{{cite journal | last = Breeden | first = Douglas | date = September 1979 | title = An intertemporal asset pricing model | journal = Journal of Financial Economics | volume = 7 | issue = 3 | pages = 265–296 }}</ref>
|-
| '''[[Fama–French three-factor model]]'''
| Size and Value factors
| Incorporates anomalies like the size and value effect not explained by standard beta.<ref name="FamaFrench1993" />
|-
| '''Co-skewness CAPM'''
| Higher-order moments
| Includes co-skewness as a priced factor, acknowledging skewness preference.<ref name="Post20082">{{cite journal |last1=Post |first1=T. |last2=Vliet |first2=P. V. |year=2008 |title=Downside Risk and Asset Pricing |journal=Journal of Banking & Finance |volume=32 |issue=10 |pages=2323–2340 |doi=10.1016/j.jbankfin.2008.01.008}}</ref>
|-
| '''[[Behavioral portfolio theory]]'''
| Mental accounting
| Proposes that humans hold fragmented portfolios based on specific psychological goals.<ref>{{cite journal |last=De Brouwer |first=Ph. |year=2009 |title=Maslowian Portfolio Theory |journal=Journal of Asset Management |volume=9 |issue=6 |pages=359–365 }}</ref>
|}

Investors with longer-term outlooks might optimally choose long-term inflation-linked bonds instead of short-term rates, suggesting that the relevant risk-free rate depends on the investor's horizon.<ref name="Campbell2002" />
